question: Should I pay only the minimum on my credit card, or a fixed amount?

source.title: Paying only the minimum on a credit card
source.publisher: Test fixture (Explain, Simulate, Decide repo); the numbers are illustrative
quotes: Credit cards make it easy to pay only the minimum each month, often 2% of the balance or $25, whichever is more.
A typical card charges about 22% a year, which works out to just under 2% a month on whatever you still owe.
Paying the minimum, it would take over 20 years to clear, and you would pay far more in interest than you originally borrowed.
Paying a fixed $200 a month instead clears the same balance in about two and a half years, with roughly $1,400 in interest.
Many people believe the minimum payment is set so that you will pay off the card in a reasonable time.
Stopping new spending on the card matters too: new purchases add to the balance faster than small payments can reduce it.
Each month the interest is added to your balance.

explain.caption: Paying only the minimum: how long until your card is clear?
This jar is what you owe on the card.
Each month the card company adds interest to what you owe.
The minimum payment is a small share of what you owe.
But the minimum barely beats the interest, so the debt hardly shrinks.
A fixed payment that doesn't shrink pays the debt down faster.
New purchases add to the debt faster than small payments remove it.
So on the minimum, the debt is still there years later.
Now make it yours. Answer a few questions.

simulate.prompt: Try your own balance, rate and payment.

tradeoffs: The minimum leaves more cash free each month, but the debt lasts far longer and costs far more in interest.
A fixed payment clears the card sooner, but it takes the same amount from your budget every month, even in a tight one.
Moving the balance to a card with a lower rate or a 0% offer can cut the interest, but there may be a transfer fee and a higher rate when the offer ends.
Stopping new purchases on the card helps the balance fall, but it means paying for things another way.
leftOut: Interest is worked out once a month here; real cards often charge it daily. At 22% a year, $200 a month works out nearer $1,750 in interest than the article's rounded $1,400.
Fees, such as late fees, annual fees and balance transfer fees, are not included.
The rate is held fixed; real rates can change, and a 0% offer ends after a set time. Check what applies to your card.
Missed or late payments, and their effect on your credit record, are not modelled.
The $100, $300 and new-purchase amounts in the questions are examples, not figures from the article.
questionsToAsk: How is my minimum payment worked out, and how long would it take to clear my balance paying only that?
What interest rate am I paying now, and is a lower rate available to me?
If I move my balance to another card, what is the fee, and what rate applies when the offer ends?
Can I set up an automatic fixed payment each month?
